questions.question: A native library caches the `JNIEnv*` from `JNI_OnLoad` in a global and uses it later from a worker thread. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, as long as the cached global variable is declared `static`
A JNIEnv is valid only on its own thread; each thread needs its own
The JNIEnv expires after a few seconds and must be refreshed by native code
The JNIEnv must first be wrapped in a global reference before it is cached
questions.explanation: A `JNIEnv` holds thread-local state such as the local reference table, so it may only be used on its own thread. Cache the `JavaVM*` instead and call `GetEnv` or `AttachCurrentThread` on the worker. Global references apply to `jobject`s, not to the env pointer.

questions.question: A thread created with `pthread_create` in C++ needs to call back into a Kotlin object. What must it do?
options: Call `AttachCurrentThread` on the JavaVM, and detach before the thread exits
Call `FindClass` first, which attaches the calling native thread automatically
Nothing special; any native thread in the process can already make JNI calls
Post the call over to the main thread, because only the main thread may use JNI
questions.explanation: Native threads are unknown to the VM until attached, and attaching gives them a `JNIEnv`. Not detaching before the thread exits leaks the thread's VM state and is reported as an error. Any attached thread can use JNI, so there is no main-thread requirement.

questions.question: A `jobject` passed into a native method can be saved in a static C++ variable and safely used in a later, separate JNI call.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Arguments and objects returned by JNI functions are local references, valid only until the native method returns on that thread. To keep an object across calls, create a global reference with `NewGlobalRef` and delete it with `DeleteGlobalRef` when done.

questions.question: This native loop crashes with a local reference table overflow for large inputs. What is the right fix?
options: Call `NewGlobalRef` on each string so it is not counted as a local reference
Run the loop on a separate attached thread that has a fresh JNIEnv and table
Call `DeleteLocalRef` on each string once stored, or use Push/PopLocalFrame
Raise the app's heap limit with `android:largeHeap` in the manifest
questions.explanation: Local references are freed only when the native method returns, so creating one per iteration fills the table. Deleting each one after `SetObjectArrayElement`, or wrapping iterations in `PushLocalFrame`/`PopLocalFrame`, keeps the count bounded. Global references would just leak in a different table, and heap size is unrelated.

questions.question: `FindClass("com/app/Callback")` works inside a JNI method called from Kotlin but returns null on a native thread you attached yourself. Why?
options: Attached threads can only find classes that ship in the Android framework itself
R8 removed the class because it was only ever referenced from native code
Attached threads must use dotted names such as `com.app.Callback` instead
It falls back to the system class loader, which cannot see your app's classes
questions.explanation: FindClass uses the class loader of the Java method on top of the stack; a freshly attached thread has none, so it falls back to the system loader. The usual fix is to look up and cache the `jclass` as a global reference in `JNI_OnLoad`, or keep a reference to the app's ClassLoader. R8 removal would fail on both threads, and JNI uses slash-separated names.

questions.question: An image filter calls a tiny native function once per pixel from Kotlin. It is slower than the pure Kotlin version. What is the best fix?
options: Annotate the native method with `@FastNative` to remove most of the call overhead
Cross once per image, passing all pixels as an array or a direct ByteBuffer
Call the native function from a background thread pool instead of the caller
Rewrite the calling loop in Java, since Kotlin adds extra overhead to JNI calls
questions.explanation: Every JNI transition costs much more than a normal call, and per-pixel calls also stop the JIT from optimizing the loop. Moving the whole loop to native code and crossing the boundary once amortizes that cost. Threads only spread the overhead around, and Java versus Kotlin makes no difference to JNI.

questions.question: Which statements about sharing array memory between Java and native code are true? Select all that apply.
options: Memory allocated with `malloc` in native code is freed by the GC when no Java object refers to it
`GetByteArrayElements` may return a copy, so native writes become visible in Java only after `ReleaseByteArrayElements`
Between `GetPrimitiveArrayCritical` and its release, you should not call other JNI functions or block
A direct ByteBuffer's memory can be moved by the GC, so its address must be fetched again on every call
questions.explanation: The VM may copy or pin an array for `Get<Type>ArrayElements`, so release with the right mode to copy changes back. Critical sections may stall the GC, which is why they must stay short and make no other JNI calls. A direct ByteBuffer's address is stable, and the GC never frees native `malloc` memory; native code owns it.

questions.question: `jmethodID` and `jfieldID` values can be looked up once and cached, and stay valid as long as their class is not unloaded.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Method and field IDs are not references and are not tied to a thread, so caching them (often in `JNI_OnLoad`) avoids repeated lookups. They become invalid only if the class is unloaded, which is rare for app classes on Android.

questions.question: Your app bundle includes `.so` files for arm64-v8a, armeabi-v7a, x86 and x86_64. How does Play keep download size down?
options: It compresses all four ABIs together and the device extracts only its own
It strips the native libraries and the device compiles the C++ during install
It serves split APKs holding only the libraries for the device's ABI
It converts every library to arm64-v8a, since all current devices support it
questions.explanation: App bundles let Play generate split APKs per ABI, so a device gets only the native code it can run. Devices never compile C++ on install. Not every device or emulator is arm64, which is why multiple ABIs are built in the first place.

questions.question: Which statements about exceptions across the JNI boundary are correct? Select all that apply.
options: If the native method returns with a Java exception pending, it is thrown in the Kotlin caller
A C++ exception thrown in native code is automatically turned into a Java exception
After a JNI call that can throw, check `ExceptionCheck` before making most other JNI calls
A pending Java exception immediately stops the native function, like a throw in Kotlin
questions.explanation: A Java exception raised during a JNI call is only marked pending; native code keeps running, must check for it, and may only call a few JNI functions until it is cleared or the method returns. On return, the pending exception is thrown in the caller. C++ exceptions are not translated and must be caught before crossing back into the VM.
